notes.summary: These Tier 2 questions test critical thinking (what logically follows, strong vs weak arguments) and emotional and social intelligence (the most mature response in a situation). Choose the calm, fair, constructive option.

concepts.title: Critical thinking
concepts.body: Separate what is stated from what is assumed. "All who trained got a bonus" does not mean "everyone with a bonus trained". A strong argument is relevant, important and directly linked to the question.

concepts.title: Emotional intelligence
concepts.body: Know and manage your own feelings: stay calm, accept mistakes, learn from failure, and respond rather than react.

concepts.title: Social intelligence
concepts.body: Understand others and work well with them: listen, include people, solve conflicts fairly and respect everyone.

varieties.name: Logical inference and arguments
varieties.how: Accept only what the facts guarantee; reject arguments based on likes, popularity or extremes.

example.q: All toppers revise daily. Asha revises daily. Is Asha a topper?
steps: The rule goes one way only: topper → revises.
Revising daily does not prove she is a topper.

varieties.name: Emotional intelligence
varieties.how: Pick the option that is calm, honest and focused on improvement.

example.q: You get a low score in a mock test. Best response?
example.answer: Review mistakes and adjust your study plan

varieties.name: Social intelligence
varieties.how: Pick the option that includes others, listens and solves the problem fairly.

example.q: A teammate is struggling with a task. Best action?
example.answer: Offer help and share what you know

tips: Avoid extreme options (shouting, quitting, ignoring) in situation questions.
In argument questions, "everyone likes it" or "it is fashionable" is a weak argument.
traps: Do not reverse a rule: "If A then B" does not give "If B then A".
The "nicest" option is not always right; the best option also solves the problem.

questions.q: In a meeting, your colleague presents your work as his own. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Shout at him in front of everyone
Talk to him calmly in private, and inform the manager with facts if needed
Stop working with him for ever
Say nothing but complain about him to others
questions.solution:
Shouting or gossip harms everyone and avoiding him does not fix the problem.
A calm private talk, with facts shared with the manager if needed, protects your work and keeps the relationship professional.

questions.q: A new student in your class sits alone during lunch every day. What should you do?
options: Ignore the student; it is not your concern
Tell others that the student is unfriendly
Invite the student to join your group
Wait for the teacher to do something
questions.solution:
Including a newcomer is the socially intelligent choice.
Inviting the student helps them feel welcome; the other options leave them isolated.

questions.q: All employees who completed the training received a bonus. Ravi received a bonus. Which of the following is definitely true?
options: Ravi completed the training
Ravi may or may not have completed the training
Ravi did not complete the training
Only Ravi received a bonus
questions.solution:
The rule says: training → bonus. It does not say bonus → training.
Others may get a bonus for other reasons.
So Ravi may or may not have completed the training.

questions.q: You fail an important exam despite working hard. Which is the most emotionally intelligent response?
options: Decide that exams are unfair and stop preparing
Blame your teachers for the result
Analyse your mistakes and make a better plan for the next attempt
Pretend it does not matter to you
questions.solution:
Accepting the result and learning from it is a mature response.
Blaming others, quitting or hiding feelings does not help improvement.

questions.q:
Question: Should mobile phones be banned inside classrooms?
Arguments:
I. Yes, phones distract students during lessons.
II. No, all students like to have their phones.
options: Only argument I is strong
Only argument II is strong
Both arguments are strong
Neither argument is strong
questions.solution:
I is directly linked to learning in class and is important: strong.
II is based only on what students like, not on any real benefit: weak.
Only I is strong.

questions.q: You lead a team. Two members strongly disagree about how to finish a project, and the deadline is near. What is the best action?
options: Pick the plan of the senior member without discussion
Let them argue until one gives up
Listen to both, compare the plans against the goal and deadline, decide, and explain the reason
Do the whole project yourself
questions.solution:
A good leader hears both sides, decides on clear criteria and explains the decision.
This solves the conflict fairly and keeps the team working together before the deadline.

flashcards.back: No. Reversing the rule is a common logical error.
Relevant, important and directly linked to the question; not based on likes or popularity.
Calm, fair, solves the problem, respects everyone.
